“London Crime Down 14%?”
What a Load of Political Bull Dung

The figure for total recorded crime is just 3%—while stalking, sexual offences and domestic-related violence with injury increased.

By Steve English  |  23 July 2026

Today’s headlines are screaming that London crime has collapsed, London is safe, and anyone saying otherwise is spreading lies.

It is blatant statistical spin.

The loudly advertised 50% reduction is not crime across London.

It is phone theft in the West End—one particular offence in one heavily policed tourist area.

The Met’s equally celebrated 14% fall does not cover all crime either. It combines selected “neighbourhood offences”, principally theft from the person, personal robbery and vehicle crime.

The published figure for all recorded crime across London is a fall of just 3%.

That is 916,176 recorded offences compared with 943,843 during the previous 12-month period.

And while high-volume theft offences fell, several far more serious categories moved in the opposite direction:

+14.3%Stalking and harassment
+5.3%Sexual offences
+0.4%Domestic-related violence with injury

Violent offences also rose from 27.8% to 30.2% of all recorded crime in London.

So thousands of fewer stolen phones and vehicle offences drag down the overall total, while increases in sexual offences, stalking and domestic violence are quietly buried beneath the celebration.

And remember: these are only crimes recorded by the police.

They do not include crimes victims never report, offences the police fail to record, or incidents people no longer bother reporting because they believe nothing will be done.

  • Phone theft in one part of central London: down 50%.
  • Selected neighbourhood offences: down 14%.
  • Total recorded crime across London: down just 3%.

But apparently, if politicians and newspapers shout the biggest and most favourable number loudly enough, they hope nobody will bother reading what it actually refers to.

This isn’t honest reporting.
It is political propaganda disguised as crime statistics.

The comparison they leave out

London is repeatedly compared with Paris, Berlin and New York, then presented as one of the safest cities in the world. Widen the comparison to other Western capitals that are usually left out, and the boast looks rather different.

London55.32026 crime index
Wellington33.32026 crime index
Warsaw25.42026 crime index

On the same survey’s measure of violent crime such as assault and armed robbery, London scores 58.15, compared with just 14.32 for Warsaw.

Numbeo is a perception-based city index rather than a table of police-recorded offences. Its value here is that it applies the same questions and scale across cities. It should not be used to prove the cause of the difference—but it plainly shows that the “one of the safest cities in the world” boast depends heavily on which cities are selected for comparison.

Sources

  1. Metropolitan Police press release — confirms the 14% figure covers selected neighbourhood offences and the 50% claim concerns phone theft in the West End.
  2. Greater London Authority: State of London — Crime — confirms the 3% total recorded-crime fall, the change in violent crime’s share, and increases in stalking and harassment, sexual offences, and domestic-related violence with injury.
  3. HMICFRS: Police improve crime recording, but many crimes left unrecorded — reports an estimated 285,000 crimes not recorded nationally.
  4. HMICFRS full crime-recording report — gives the estimated national recording rate of 94.8%.
  5. Office for National Statistics: Crime in England and Wales, year ending March 2026 — provides reporting-rate and Crime Survey context.
  6. Numbeo: Crime in London — current city index and violent-crime perception measure.
  7. Numbeo: Crime Index by City 2026 — includes Wellington’s 2026 crime and safety index.
  8. Numbeo: Crime in Warsaw — current city index and violent-crime perception measure.
Period note: the Met’s 14% neighbourhood-crime figure covers the 12 months to June 2026. The GLA’s 3% total-notifiable-offence figure covers April 2025 to March 2026. They are not the same measure or precisely the same reporting window; the key point is that the heavily promoted 14% figure is not an overall London crime figure.
